extracted.intended_audience: Title IX coordinators, school administrators, legal counsel, and institutional officials responsible for implementing Title IX supportive measures (K-12 and postsecondary institutions)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative standards for providing, modifying, disclosing, and reviewing supportive measures under 34 CFR §106.44(g), including limits on burdens, procedural protections for challenges, confidentiality, and distinctions from emergency removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures must not unreasonably burden either party
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(g)(2) clarifies that supportive measures must not unreasonably burden either party and must be designed to protect the safety of the parties or the recipient's educational environment or to provide support during the recipient's grievance procedures under §106.45 (and, if applicable, §106.46) or the informal resolution process under §106.44(k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recipient may provide measures that impose some burden on the other party, but such burdens cannot be unreasonable; the unreasonableness determination must account for the nature of educational programs, activities, opportunities, and benefits in which the party participates (not solely academic components). Examples: schedule or housing adjustments may or may not be unreasonable; suspension or expulsion are inherently unreasonable as supportive measures. The Department declines to provide an exhaustive list so recipients retain case-by-case flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures must not be imposed for punitive or disciplinary reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department changed 'may' to 'must' to emphasize that a recipient must not impose supportive measures for punitive or disciplinary reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A punitive/disciplinary measure is intended to punish a respondent for conduct that violates Title IX, whereas a supportive measure is intended to fulfill the purposes in §106.2 (restore/preserve access, provide safety/support). If a party can show a supportive measure was intended to punish (e.g., did not remedy barriers to access), the recipient must terminate the measure. Actions available as disciplinary sanctions after a determination of responsibility are not inherently disciplinary when used as supportive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures must be reasonably available
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department modified wording in rulemaking from 'available and reasonable' to 'reasonably available' (and aligns §106.44(g)(2) to require measures that are not unreasonably burdensome and are designed to protect safety or provide support during grievance procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients have discretion to make case-specific judgments about whether actions comply with the definition of supportive measures and whether they are reasonably available given the institution's context and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must undertake fact-specific inquiry when assessing burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department expects recipients to engage in a fact-specific inquiry to determine whether supportive measures constitute a reasonable burden on a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the unique circumstances of parties and the nature of educational programs/activities. Recipients should weigh whether a measure restores or preserves access, protects safety, or provides support during the grievance process. Department declined to mandate a specific test or exhaustive examples to preserve institutional flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures are distinct from emergency removal and do not require the emergency risk analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures can be provided to restore or preserve access and protect safety without the individualized safety and risk analysis required for emergency removal under §106.44(h), which is only for imminent and serious threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should use §106.44(h) emergency removal only when a respondent poses an imminent and serious threat and the risk assessment threshold is met. Supportive measures can be used more flexibly to preserve access and safety without meeting that threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification or termination of supportive measures at conclusion of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(g)(3) directs recipients to, as appropriate, modify or terminate supportive measures at the conclusion of grievance procedures under §106.45 (and if applicable §106.46) or informal resolution under §106.44(k); recipients may also continue measures beyond conclusion when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should reassess whether measures continue to meet the definition of supportive measures after proceedings conclude, especially following a finding of non-responsibility (which often constitutes a materially changed circumstance requiring modification or termination). Parties may seek modification/termination under §106.44(g)(4) if circumstances materially change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures are not 'relevant evidence' in determinations of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department clarifies that supportive measures are not 'relevant evidence' that can be considered in reaching a determination under §106.45(b)(6) and (h)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information about whether a party received supportive measures should not be used as evidence bearing on responsibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties may challenge supportive measures 'applicable to them'
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(g)(4) provides that a complainant or respondent may challenge a recipient's decision to provide, deny, modify, or terminate supportive measures only when such measures are 'applicable to them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a complainant requests a transfer out of a class, that measure is not applicable to the respondent, so the respondent need not be afforded an opportunity to challenge it. Conversely, measures that apply to both parties (e.g., stay-away orders) are challengeable by either party as applicable to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely opportunity for independent review by an appropriate and impartial employee
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must provide a party with a timely opportunity to seek, from an appropriate and impartial employee, modification or reversal of the recipient's challenged decision regarding supportive measures applicable to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The impartial reviewer may modify or reverse the challenged decision when it is inconsistent with the definition of 'supportive measures' in §106.2. The Department deleted language requiring a formal 'fact-specific inquiry' about timeliness to avoid implying a formal process; recipients have flexibility to determine what constitutes timely and may use informal procedures. The initial opportunity need not always be provided before the measure is imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible bases for challenging supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department added language clarifying that challenges may include whether a supportive measure is reasonably burdensome, reasonably available, imposed for punitive or disciplinary reasons, imposed without fee or charge, and whether the measure is effective in meeting its intended purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bases are illustrative, not exhaustive. An impartial employee may consider any of these grounds when determining whether to modify or reverse a recipient's decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient must provide independent review but not an entire new administrative structure
rubrics_metrics.description: While §106.44(g)(4) requires an impartial employee to review challenges, it does not mandate a large administrative apparatus; at minimum one person with authority to modify/reverse decisions must be assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may delegate provision of supportive measures and designate a different impartial administrator to review challenges. However, the same person cannot both provide and review the same supportive measures (to ensure independence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients retain discretion; not required to equalize or mirror measures for both parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to require recipients to equalize the application of supportive measures or to minimize the combined burden by taking on burdens themselves; supportive measures should be individualized and based on necessity to restore/preserve access, protect safety, or provide support during procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandating identical measures for both parties could be unnecessary and burdensome (e.g., providing escort services to both when only one requires it). Recipients must, however, consider alternative measures and avoid imposing measures at the expense of considering less burdensome options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and limits on disclosure of supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(g)(5) limits the recipient's disclosure of supportive measures, generally restricting disclosure to the parties unless disclosure is necessary to restore or preserve that party's access to the education program or activity; §106.44(j) protects personally identifiable information obtained in complying with this part and exceptions in §106.44(j)(1)-(5) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information about the supportive measure itself (not just identity of parties) is protected; for example, a respondent may know who the complainant is but is not entitled to know that the complainant is receiving counseling. Commenters raised potential conflicts with reporting obligations (e.g., CHIPS/Science Act or federal grant terms) and parental notification; §106.44(g)(5) permits disclosure where an exception in §106.44(j) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients need not proactively monitor and affirmatively modify supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to require recipients to affirmatively modify supportive measures or initiate new measures proactively; instead, parties who believe a measure is ineffective or circumstances have materially changed may seek modification under §106.44(g)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive monitoring of all outstanding supportive measures would be extremely burdensome. The challenge process exists to address ineffectiveness or materially changed circumstances.
